s01_intro: In the last video we drew a bracket plate in Onshape and exported it as a D X F. Now we'll open that file in Inkscape, prepare it for the laser, and add some text. This is the step that decides whether the laser cuts your part or just scratches it.
s02_import: First, open the file. Go to File, Open, and pick the D X F you exported from Onshape. Inkscape asks how to scale it. The safest choice is Read from file, which trusts the units recorded in the file. Our drawing is one hundred millimetres by sixty, and it opens at exactly that.
s03_hairline: First, the line width. Select everything in the drawing: Edit, Select All in All Layers. Then open Object, Fill and Stroke. On the Stroke style tab, set the width to Hairline. The laser follows the centre of a line, so a thick line gives it nothing useful to follow.
s04_nopaint: Next the fill. Stay in Fill and Stroke, open the Fill tab, and click the X to set it to No paint. A filled shape is not a cut, it's an engraving. Now the outlines are ready, so let's group them: press Control G, and the plate behaves as one object.
s05_red: Now the colour, and this is the important part. The laser decides what to do by the colour of each line. Red means cut all the way through. Open the Stroke paint tab, choose Flat color, and set the values to red two five five, green zero, blue zero. Check that opacity is one hundred percent. A semi transparent line is a different colour as far as the laser is concerned.
s06_etched: Now let's add something to etch. Etching is a surface mark, not a cut, and the laser reads black as etch. Pick the Text tool, or just press T, and click in the middle of the plate. Type E N T dash one six four. Then set this text to pure black, zero, zero, zero, and no stroke, so it etches rather than cuts.
s07_center: The text landed roughly where we clicked, but we want it exactly centred on the plate. Press Control Alt A to select everything. Now open Object, Align and Distribute. Click Centre on the horizontal axis, then Centre on the vertical axis. The text snaps to the middle of the plate.
s08_save: One more step, and it's one people forget. Text and drawings are not the same kind of object to the laser, so convert the text to a path. With the text selected, open the Path menu and choose Object to Path. The text becomes ordinary vector outlines that any machine can follow. Save the file, and it's ready for the laser cutter.
s09_recap: That's the workflow. Open your D X F at the right scale. Set the stroke to hairline and the fill to no paint. Make your cuts pure red and your etch lines pure black. Centre anything you add, convert text to paths, and save. Next time you're at Nolop, you'll open this file in U C P and send it to the laser. Happy making.
